name: Ramona Zertuche
equipment: Buckskin coat, fringed, smoked dark, made by her grandmother
Repeating rifle (Winchester '66), 12 rounds loaded, in a tooled scabbard
Navy revolver (converted to cartridge), 6 rounds loaded, in a belt holster
Lariat, rawhide, sixty feet, braided by her father
Leather leggings (chivarras) against the brush, and big roweled spurs
Saddle and tack (a Mexican saddle with a horn the size of a saucer), bedroll, canteen (3)
Cow pony: a quick dun mare called La Prieta
A copy of her family's 1767 grant, the porción of El Saucito, in a tin tube, and a lawyer's bill from Brownsville for $310
features: Both Sides of the River (Borderlands origin: English and Spanish natively; she knows the fords, trails and towns on both sides of the border, and in any borderland town she can find someone who knows her family; advantage on Persuasion and Insight checks with people of either side who live along the border; she can always find a guide, a ford or a place to sleep there)

Trailcraft (Scout: never lost on terrain she has crossed before; on any terrain she finds water for herself, her companions and the horses each day without a check wherever there is any within a day's travel; she can follow a trail at a normal pace and read how many riders, how long ago, and whether the horses were shod, loaded or lame; her party cannot become lost while she guides it except by storm or deliberate deception)

Long Shot (Scout: attacking at long range with a Longarm does not impose disadvantage on her if she Aimed first that turn; her proficiency bonus is doubled for Perception checks to spot something more than 300 ft away)

Ghost on the Range (Scout, 2nd level: in natural terrain she can Hide as a bonus action, even when only lightly obscured; travel pace never imposes disadvantage on her Stealth; she leaves no trail anyone without Trailcraft can follow unless she chooses to)
Path: Guide (Scout, 3rd level: her party travels at a hard pace without exhaustion, finds forage for its horses on any terrain that has any, and has advantage on saves against weather)

The Trail Outfit (Cattle Drover background: any trail crew, ranch bunkhouse or cow-town saloon will take her in for a night, and a trail boss short of hands will hire her on sight at $30 a month and found; she knows the trails, the crossings and who in each town cheats drovers)

personality.traits: I correct people when they mispronounce rivers. I sing to horses and argue with cattle. I laugh at men who think they invented the lariat. I go quiet when I'm angry, and I'm angry about once a day.
personality.ideals: The land belongs to the people who have worked it, and paper belongs to the people who can read it. I intend to be both.
personality.bonds: El Saucito, my family's rancho on the river above Laredo, held under a Spanish grant since 1767. A Brownsville lawyer for an Anglo speculator says our survey is defective. Our own lawyer says he can win it for six hundred dollars more, and the appeal will cost another thousand. Two thousand dollars is the rancho.
personality.flaws: I have been telling myself that this is just a man on a poster and that I'm only doing what every bounty hunter does. When I find out who his wife's people are, I am going to have to stop telling myself that.

appearance: A small, wiry, brown woman of twenty-seven with a sharp face, a wide mouth, black hair in one long braid under a low-crowned grey sombrero, and a squint from a lifetime of looking at horizons. Buckskin coat, leather leggings, big spurs that ring when she walks, a rifle she carries like an extension of her arm.
backstory: Ramona Zertuche was born on El Saucito, a cattle and horse rancho on the Texas bank of the Rio Grande above Laredo, the third of seven children, and rode before she walked. Her father, Don Anselmo, taught her everything a vaquero knows; her mother taught her to keep the accounts, which is how she found out in 1872 that a Brownsville lawyer representing an Anglo land company had filed suit claiming half the rancho on a defect in the 1767 survey. Since then she has hired out as a trail hand, a mustanger and a tracker from the Nueces to the Pecos, sending money home to pay the family's own lawyer, and she has learned to track men as well as cattle, because men pay better. She took the poster off a stage station wall at Seguin because two thousand dollars is the whole of the lawsuit and the appeal. She has crossed the Wild Horse Desert four times. She knows the Rio Grande country from Laredo to the Gulf, and she knows the Cantú families of the river by reputation, as everyone on the border does; she does not yet know that the man on the poster married one of them.
